content.intro: This page is built around one worked example: an 8-week, $180,000 back-to-school campaign across eight lines, from Meta and TikTok to CTV, search and digital out-of-home. Every number in it is calculated from the line above it, so you can check the method as well as copy the layout. The download has the same example, a blank plan with the formulas in place, and a flowchart tab that fills itself in from your flight dates.
content.how_it_works: Enter a total budget and the share for each of four core channels to see the dollar split. Use it to rough out the mix before you fill in the template line by line. The four channels here usually take 65–95% of a plan; the rest goes to audio, out-of-home, retail media or influencer lines.

faq.question: What is a media plan template?
faq.answer: A spreadsheet laid out to record a paid media campaign line by line: what runs (channel, tactic, vendor), when (flight dates), what it costs (budget, CPM or CPC) and what it should deliver (impressions, reach, frequency, KPI). A good one calculates impressions and totals for you and includes a **flowchart** tab showing spend by week.

faq.question: What should a media plan include?
faq.answer: At the top: the campaign objective, target audience, audience size, total budget and dates. Then one row per line item with channel, tactic or placement, vendor, flight start and end, budget, rate (CPM, CPC or flat), impressions, estimated reach, frequency, KPI and notes. Underneath: totals, blended CPM, combined reach and a weekly flowchart. Creative specs and a measurement plan usually sit in separate documents that reference the plan.

faq.question: What is a media flowchart?
faq.answer: The week-by-week view of a media plan: line items down the side, weeks across the top, and a shaded bar (often with the weekly spend) for each week a line is live. It shows pacing, overlap between channels and gaps in the schedule at a glance. In this template it is the **Flowchart** tab, built from the flight dates on the plan tab.

faq.question: How do you calculate impressions in a media plan?
faq.answer: **Impressions = budget / CPM × 1,000.** In the example, $45,000 on Meta at a $9 CPM is 45,000 / 9 × 1,000 = **5,000,000 impressions**. Blended CPM for the whole plan is total budget / total impressions × 1,000: $180,000 / 14,850,000 × 1,000 = **$12.12**.

faq.question: How do you estimate total reach across channels?
faq.answer: You can't add reach across lines, because the same people see several channels. The template uses the random-duplication estimate: **combined reach = audience × (1 − the product of (1 − line reach / audience))**. In the example that gives about 3.73 million people, 46.6% of an 8 million audience, at an average frequency of 4.0. Platform reach planners and cross-media tools model overlap more precisely.

faq.question: How do I put CPC or CPV buys into a CPM-based plan?
faq.answer: Convert them to an effective CPM. The example's search line spends $24,000 at a $1.50 CPC, which buys 16,000 clicks; at an 8% CTR that is 200,000 impressions, so the effective CPM is 24,000 / 200,000 × 1,000 = **$120**. Enter $120 as the CPM and record the buy type in the notes.

faq.question: Does the template work in Google Sheets or Numbers?
faq.answer: Yes. Upload the .xlsx to Google Drive and open it with Google Sheets, or open it in Numbers; the formulas carry over. The CSV holds the worked example as plain values, for importing into another tool or a database.

faq.question: When should I move from a spreadsheet to a media planning tool?
faq.answer: A spreadsheet is fine for one campaign and one planner. Once you have several flights running at once, more than one person editing, or need planned vs delivered vs billed in one place, a dedicated media planning tool saves more time than it costs. The directory on this site compares them.
